name: Push-ups
summary: How many push-ups you can do in a row without resting, with good form. It measures the endurance of the chest, shoulder and upper-arm muscles, and depends on body weight, technique and motivation.
howTo: Warm up for a few minutes first.
Choose one version and keep it every time: from the toes (standard) or from the knees (modified). The norms for the two are different, so record which one you did.
Hands about shoulder-width apart, directly under the shoulders, fingers pointing forward. Body straight and stiff from head to heels (or head to knees); hips neither sagging nor raised.

Lower yourself until your chest is about a fist's height from the floor (in the CSEP/ACE protocol the chest touches the tester's fist, a rolled towel or a foam block), without resting your stomach on the floor.
Push back up until the elbows are straight. That is one push-up.
Keep going at a steady pace with no rest. Count only complete push-ups with good form.
Stop when you cannot do another complete push-up, or when your form breaks down on two push-ups in a row (ACE/CSEP rule). Write down the number and the version.
For later comparisons, test at a similar time of day, rested, and not right after other upper-body exercise.
safety: Stop at once if you feel chest pain, dizziness, light-headedness or unusual shortness of breath (the stop symptoms used in Yang et al. 2019), and contact a doctor if it happens.
If you have heart disease, high blood pressure that is not under control, or have been told to avoid strenuous effort, check with your doctor before testing to exhaustion.
The test may not suit people with shoulder, elbow or wrist problems (ACE contraindications); a doctor or physiotherapist can suggest an alternative.
A test to exhaustion depends on motivation; a person new to exercise may stop early, and a person pushing too hard may lose form and strain a joint.

norms.label: Canada (CSEP)

source.title: The Canadian Physical Activity, Fitness & Lifestyle Approach (CPAFLA): CSEP-Health & Fitness Program's Health-Related Appraisal and Counselling Strategy
source.note: 3rd edition, Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology, Ottawa. Book; not read in the original. The same table is said to be reproduced in ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription (Wolters Kluwer); not checked.

norms.verifiedFrom: secondary website: American Council on Exercise, 'ACE Group Fitness Instructor Fitness Assessment Protocols', Table 3 'Fitness Categories for the Push-up by Age and Sex', printed as 'Reprinted with permission from Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology (2003)' (https://www.acefitness.org/groupfitnessresources/pdfs/GFI_Assessments.pdf, read 2026-10-29). Cross-checked against https://www.sensai.fit/blog/push-up-test-norms-by-age-sex (same numbers, with >= and <= signs).
norms.population: Canadian adults; the sample (size, years, how chosen) is not documented in any source I could read. ACE says only that the table comes from CPAFLA 2003.
norms.note: Men: standard push-ups from the toes. Women: modified push-ups from the knees (not comparable with the men's numbers or with women's push-ups from the toes). The ACE PDF prints Excellent and Needs improvement as bare numbers (e.g. '36', '16'); they are read as 'at least' and 'at most' because the bands in between are contiguous and sensai.fit prints them as >=36 and <=16. DISCREPANCY: for women 60-69, ACE prints Excellent as '14', which overlaps its own Very good band 12-16; sensai.fit prints >=17. 17 is used here; check against the CPAFLA or ACSM book before shipping. No 15-19 band was found in any readable source (ACSM's book may have one; not added from memory). No band above 69. The categories are labels from the norm set, not health thresholds; no study ties them to health outcomes. Women aged 60–69, Excellent: one reprint prints 14, which overlaps its own Very good band (12–16); the other prints 17, used here.

evidence.claim: In male firefighters in Indiana (USA), aged about 21 to 66 (average 40), those who could do more push-ups at a check-up had fewer heart and blood vessel events over the next 10 years. Men who did 41 or more had far fewer events than men who did 10 or fewer.
whyThisGrade: Observational: shows a link, not that push-ups prevent heart disease.
One group of active working men; the authors say it may not apply to women, older or inactive people.
Few events: 37 in total and 1 in the 41-or-more group, so the estimates are imprecise (IRR 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-0.36).

The push-up groups also differed in age, weight, blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking; the authors say these may explain much of the difference and that the results do not support push-ups as an independent predictor.
About a quarter of the firefighters had no push-up result; no correction for multiple comparisons.

studies.title: Association Between Push-up Exercise Capacity and Future Cardiovascular Events Among Active Adult Men

evidence.claim: In a sample of Canadian adults (men and women, 20-69 years) followed for 13 years, push-up scores showed no pattern with the risk of dying once age, smoking, body size and estimated aerobic fitness were taken into account. Sit-ups did.
whyThisGrade: Observational, one national sample measured in 1981.
238 deaths in 13 years; limited numbers could hide a small link.
Push-ups were compared in age- and sex-specific quartiles, not by the cut-offs used in norm tables.

studies.title: Musculoskeletal fitness and risk of mortality

limits: It measures upper-body muscular endurance only, not heart health, aerobic fitness or overall strength.
The result depends on how deep each push-up goes, the pace, practice and motivation; numbers done with a different technique are not comparable.
Heavier people lift more weight with each push-up, so the count partly reflects body size.
Knee push-ups and toe push-ups use different norms and are not interchangeable; converting one into the other is an estimate, not a measurement.
The CSEP norm categories come from a Canadian sample that is not described in the sources available, and they are more than 20 years old.
Evidence linking push-ups to health is limited to one study of male firefighters (a link) and one Canadian population study (no link); there is no outcome evidence for women.
A low score is not a diagnosis, and a high score does not rule out heart disease.
